title: John 3:22–36
context: Jesus and his disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes nearby. When John’s disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus, John answers that a person can receive only what is given from heaven. He is the friend of the bridegroom and rejoices to hear his voice: he must increase, and I must decrease. The chapter closes by contrasting the one from above with those from the earth. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, and whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. Both traditions find verse 36 decisive. They read verse 27 differently.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Gifts from heaven and believing the Son: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: A man can receive nothing—neither he nor I—unless it be given him from heaven. He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life. He that obeyeth not the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abideth on him. The unbeliever remains under the wrath he was under before.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 3:27, 36)

reformed.quote: John ascribes it to the providence of God that Christ has more disciples… A man can receive nothing unless it be given him from heaven. He who believes in the Son has life; he who does not obey the Son shall not see life. Faith is not in every man’s power, and yet unbelief is justly condemned, because the whole blame lies with men themselves.

verses.text: After these things, Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea. He stayed there with them and baptized.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus and his disciples went into Judea and baptized there. Arminian readers note the parallel ministries of John and Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the transition from John’s preparatory ministry to Jesus’ ministry.

verses.text: John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came and were baptized;
verses.arminianNotes: John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful. Arminian readers see John’s faithful continuance in his calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see John continuing the work God gave him.

verses.text: for John was not yet thrown into prison.
verses.arminianNotes: John had not yet been put in prison. Arminian readers see John’s eyewitness concern for chronology.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Gospel situating events within the other accounts.

verses.text: Therefore a dispute arose on the part of John’s disciples with some Jews about purification.
verses.arminianNotes: A discussion arose about purification. Arminian readers see questions about rites leading to deeper questions about Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see purification fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Everyone is going to him.” Arminian readers see John’s disciples worried about losing followers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see human jealousy contrasted with John’s humility.

verses.text: John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. Arminian readers see John accepting his limited role as God’s gift. The verse concerns ministry and calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a general principle that applies to salvation as well: everything, including faith, is a gift from heaven.
verses.keyContrast: Both see John acknowledging that his role is a gift from God. Arminian readers apply the verse mainly to ministry and calling. Reformed readers see it as stating a broad principle that includes the gift of faith.

verses.text: You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
verses.arminianNotes: I said, I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. Arminian readers see John’s faithfulness to his role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see John’s ministry as appointed by God.

verses.text: He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
verses.arminianNotes: The friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Arminian readers see joy in Christ’s success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ as bridegroom of his church, his chosen bride.

verses.text: He must increase, but I must decrease.
verses.arminianNotes: He must increase, but I must decrease. Both traditions treasure this as a model of Christian humility. Arminian readers see a call to self-giving service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see all glory belonging to Christ.

verses.text: “He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all.
verses.arminianNotes: He who comes from above is above all. Arminian readers see Christ’s supremacy over every human messenger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Son’s heavenly origin and authority.

verses.text: What he has seen and heard, of that he testifies; and no one receives his witness.
verses.arminianNotes: He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony. Arminian readers see general rejection by the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see natural humanity refusing Christ’s testimony apart from grace.

verses.text: He who has received his witness has set his seal to this, that God is true.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true. Arminian readers see faith as affirming God’s truthfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faith as confessing God’s truthfulness, a response God enables.

verses.text: For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.
verses.arminianNotes: He whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. Arminian readers see Christ fully empowered by the Spirit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Son anointed by the Spirit without limit for his mediatorial work.

verses.text: The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. Arminian readers see the Son’s authority over all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Father’s gift of all things to the Son, including his people (6:37).

verses.text: One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. Arminian readers see belief and unbelief as the decisive human response that determines one’s destiny.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wrath of God already resting on all outside Christ, with faith as the only way of deliverance.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm that faith in the Son brings eternal life and unbelief leaves people under wrath. Arminian readers stress the human response as decisive. Reformed readers stress that wrath already rests on all by nature, and only faith, God’s gift, delivers from it.
